title: How Would You Convince Leadership to Invest in a Costly Re-Architecture?
summary: Tests whether you can make a business case for an expensive, non-feature-shipping investment in terms non-technical stakeholders act on — cost, risk, and opportunity cost — not only technical justification.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"how would you convince leadership to invest in a costly re-architecture?"** "The current architecture is bad" is not itself a business case — leadership funds outcomes measured in cost, risk, and opportunity cost, not engineering aesthetics.

A strong answer translates the technical problem into terms the audience already tracks, with real numbers, and presents the re-architecture against a named alternative rather than in isolation.

Ask what the concrete, measurable pain the current architecture is causing today is — lost revenue, missed deals, engineering velocity, incident frequency. Who's the actual audience for this pitch, and what do they already care about?

Different audiences track different numbers — a CFO cares about cost and risk exposure, a product leader cares about velocity and roadmap enablement. The same technical problem needs a different framing depending on who's in the room.

Translate the technical problem into the business terms the audience already tracks — cost, risk, or speed — with real numbers, and present the re-architecture as the cheaper option relative to a named alternative, not in isolation.

"Relative to a named alternative" matters — a cost presented alone sounds arbitrary; a cost presented against "the alternative is continuing to lose $X per quarter" gives leadership an actual comparison to evaluate.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: translating outages into dollars
slides.markdown:
A worked example: instead of "our monolith is hard to maintain," present "we've had 6 Sev1 outages in the current architecture this quarter, each costing an estimated $50K in lost transactions, and our own postmortems trace 4 of them to the same underlying coupling problem that this re-architecture directly fixes."

The second framing gives leadership a number to weigh against the re-architecture's cost — a decision they can actually evaluate, versus a vague quality complaint they have no way to price.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: tying the pitch to opportunity cost
slides.markdown:
A concrete scenario: pitching a data-store migration by quantifying the *opportunity cost* of not doing it — "our current database can't support the multi-region expansion the roadmap needs for next year; without this migration, that roadmap item isn't achievable at all, not just slower."

Tying the technical investment directly to a business initiative leadership already wants reframes the ask from "spend money on infrastructure" to "unblock something you've already committed to."

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what makes the pitch credible
slides.markdown:
![Full-budget single block pitch versus a phased staircase of milestones](assets/pitch-shapes-comparison.svg)

A phased plan with a cheaper first milestone that delivers partial value quickly, rather than asking for the full budget upfront for a multi-quarter effort with no visible progress until the end, makes the pitch credible instead of speculative.

A staircase of small, real wins is easier for leadership to fund and re-evaluate at each step than a single large bet with no checkpoint until completion.

assets.alt: Full-budget single block pitch versus a phased staircase of milestones

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Framing in pure business terms risks oversimplifying real technical nuance that matters for the actual execution. Framing in pure technical terms risks losing the audience that controls the budget. The pitch has to hold both — technical accuracy for the team executing it, business framing for the people funding it.

This isn't a compromise between two languages — it's writing for two different audiences at once, each of whom needs the parts of the story relevant to their decision.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: leadership says the ROI isn't clear enough
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "leadership says the ROI isn't clear enough — what do you do?" Narrow the ask to the smallest phase that produces a measurable result, proving the case with real data before asking for the rest of the investment, rather than re-arguing the same full pitch louder.

This is the phased-plan idea from earlier, applied specifically to overcoming ROI skepticism — a small, provable win is more persuasive than a bigger, unproven promise repeated more forcefully.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: a feature deadline threatens to pull the team off
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "you get the budget, but 6 months in, a critical feature deadline threatens to pull the team off the re-architecture — how do you protect it?" The same tool as an error budget for reliability: pre-agree what a pause versus an outright cancellation looks like, and protect at minimum whatever partial milestone is already in flight rather than letting it fully unwind.

Agreeing on this before the pressure hits — not negotiating it in the moment — is what actually protects the investment when a real deadline conflict shows up.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: pitching on technical merit alone
slides.markdown:
**Wrong move:** pitching a re-architecture purely on technical merit or "best practice," without quantifying the business cost of the status quo or the cost of the alternative.

**Why it's wrong:** leadership can't weigh a decision they can't price — "this is better engineering" gives them nothing to compare against the very real, very quantifiable cost of the investment being requested.

**Correct model:** always attach a real number to the cost of not acting, and present the ask relative to that number, not as a standalone technical improvement.

Translate the technical problem into cost, risk, or speed — the terms the audience already tracks — with real numbers, and tie the ask to a business initiative leadership already wants, not an isolated infrastructure improvement. Propose a phased plan with an early, provable milestone rather than a single large ask with no visible progress.

When ROI is questioned, narrow the ask rather than re-arguing louder. See [writing-a-design-doc](writing-a-design-doc) and [cost-and-org-aware-design](cost-and-org-aware-design) for the deeper skills this pitch draws on.
